vocabulary.definition: The period from 1865 to 1877 when the United States worked to rebuild the South and define the rights of newly freed African Americans
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The war answered whether the nation would stay together — Reconstruction had to answer everything else: What does freedom actually mean? Who is a citizen? It was America's attempt to rebuild itself into something more equal than before.
vocabulary.example: During Reconstruction, formerly enslaved people opened schools, ran for office, and voted — and some served in Congress for the first time
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Reconstruction was the period from 1865 to 1877 when the nation tried to rebuild the South after the Civil War. It asked the hardest questions in American history: what does freedom mean, and who counts as a citizen? Its victories and its unfinished business still shape the country today.

vocabulary.definition: The constitutional amendment, ratified in 1868, granting citizenship to all people born in the United States and guaranteeing equal protection under the law
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The amendment that answered 'who is an American?' with 'anyone born here.' It made formerly enslaved people citizens and promised that states must treat everyone equally under the law — a promise Americans have been working to keep ever since.
vocabulary.example: The 14th Amendment overturned the Dred Scott decision by making citizenship a birthright, and it is still cited in civil rights cases today
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The 14th Amendment, ratified in 1868, granted citizenship to everyone born in the United States. It also required states to give all people equal protection under the law. More civil rights cases have been argued on this amendment than almost any other part of the Constitution.

vocabulary.definition: The constitutional amendment, ratified in 1870, prohibiting states from denying the vote based on race, color, or previous condition of servitude
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The amendment that put voting rights for Black men into the Constitution. On paper, race could no longer keep a man from the ballot box — though Southern states soon invented workarounds, which is why the gap between rights on paper and rights in real life matters so much in this unit.
vocabulary.example: After the 15th Amendment, hundreds of thousands of Black men voted, and states like Mississippi and South Carolina elected Black senators and congressmen
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The 15th Amendment, ratified in 1870, said the right to vote could not be denied because of race, color, or previous enslavement. Black men across the South registered and voted in huge numbers. Later laws and violence stripped that right away in practice, a struggle that continued into the 1960s.

vocabulary.definition: A federal agency created in 1865 to help formerly enslaved people and poor Southerners with food, medical care, schools, and legal support
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The government's first big relief agency. Four million people walked out of slavery with no land, no schools, and no legal records — the Bureau helped with food, hospitals, contracts, reuniting separated families, and above all, schools.
vocabulary.example: The Freedmen's Bureau helped establish thousands of schools and several colleges, including Howard University
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Freedmen's Bureau was a federal agency created in 1865 to help formerly enslaved people build free lives. It provided food, medical care, and legal help, and it built thousands of schools across the South. Education was its most lasting achievement, even after Congress shut the Bureau down.

vocabulary.definition: A farming system in which laborers worked a landowner's fields in exchange for a share of the crop, often trapping families in permanent debt
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Freedom without land. Formerly enslaved families farmed a landowner's fields for a share of the harvest — but after paying for tools, seed, and supplies on credit, many ended each year owing more than they earned. It kept the cotton economy running on cheap labor.
vocabulary.example: A sharecropping family might harvest a full cotton crop and still end the year in debt to the landowner's store
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Sharecropping was a system where farm families worked a landowner's fields in exchange for a share of the crop. Supplies were bought on credit, so many families ended every year deeper in debt. Economically, it kept much of the South's cotton system in place long after slavery ended.

vocabulary.definition: Laws passed by Southern states immediately after the Civil War to restrict the freedom, movement, and labor of African Americans
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Southern states' first attempt to keep things as close to slavery as possible without the name. Black Codes forced freedpeople into unfair labor contracts and limited where they could live, work, and travel — and they convinced Congress that the South needed stricter oversight.
vocabulary.example: Under some Black Codes, a Black person without a signed labor contract could be arrested and forced to work for a planter
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Black Codes were laws passed by Southern states right after the Civil War to restrict the freedom of African Americans. They controlled where freedpeople could work, live, and travel. Outrage over the codes pushed Congress to pass the 14th Amendment and take control of Reconstruction.

vocabulary.definition: A Northerner who moved to the South during Reconstruction, often accused by white Southerners of seeking profit or political power
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: An insult with a suitcase in it — the name suggests someone who packed everything into a cheap carpet bag to grab opportunity down South. Some newcomers really were profit-seekers; many others were teachers, agents, and reformers. The label itself is a lesson in perspective and bias.
vocabulary.example: A Northern teacher who moved to Georgia to teach in a Freedmen's Bureau school might be dismissed as a carpetbagger by resentful neighbors
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Carpetbagger was the insulting name white Southerners gave Northerners who moved South during Reconstruction. The word pictured an outsider arriving with everything stuffed in a carpet bag, hunting for profit or power. Historians note that many so-called carpetbaggers were actually teachers and reformers, so the label is a case study in bias.

vocabulary.definition: The process by which Congress formally charges a federal official with wrongdoing; the House impeaches, and the Senate holds the trial
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The Constitution's emergency brake on presidents and other officials. Impeachment is the accusation, not the removal — the House files the charges and the Senate decides. President Andrew Johnson, who fought Congress over Reconstruction, survived his trial by a single vote.
vocabulary.example: In 1868 Andrew Johnson became the first U.S. president to be impeached; the Senate came one vote short of removing him from office
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Impeachment is the process Congress uses to formally charge a federal official with wrongdoing. The House of Representatives brings the charges, and the Senate holds a trial. In 1868, President Andrew Johnson was impeached in his battle with Congress over Reconstruction and kept his office by one vote.

vocabulary.definition: A secret organization formed in the South after the Civil War that used violence and intimidation to stop African Americans from voting and exercising their rights
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: When laws couldn't undo Black freedom, some white Southerners turned to fear. The Klan attacked and threatened Black voters, teachers, and officeholders — and the white Southerners who worked with them — to scare people away from using their new rights. It's why rights on paper weren't enough.
vocabulary.example: Klan violence before elections was designed to keep Black citizens from the polls, until federal enforcement laws in the early 1870s cracked down on the group
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Ku Klux Klan was a secret organization that used violence and fear to fight Reconstruction. It targeted African Americans who voted, taught, or held office, along with their allies. Congress passed enforcement laws in the early 1870s to protect voters, showing that rights require protection to be real.

vocabulary.definition: The political deal that settled the disputed 1876 election: Rutherford B. Hayes became president, and federal troops were withdrawn from the South, ending Reconstruction
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The backroom deal that ended Reconstruction. The 1876 election was too close to call, so Democrats let Hayes take the White House — and in exchange, the last federal troops protecting Black rights left the South. Rebuilding stopped mid-project.
vocabulary.example: After the Compromise of 1877 pulled troops out, Southern states rapidly stripped away the voting power Black citizens had built during Reconstruction
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Compromise of 1877 settled the disputed presidential election of 1876. Rutherford B. Hayes became president, and in return the last federal troops were withdrawn from the South. That withdrawal ended Reconstruction and left Black Southerners without federal protection for their rights.

vocabulary.definition: State and local laws that enforced racial segregation in the South from the late 1800s into the 1960s
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: What filled the space Reconstruction left behind. Jim Crow laws legally separated Black and white Americans in schools, trains, restaurants, and nearly every public space — 'separate but equal' in name, deeply unequal in fact. Tearing them down took the civil rights movement nearly a century later.
vocabulary.example: Under Jim Crow laws, a Black traveler in the South had to use separate rail cars, waiting rooms, and water fountains
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Jim Crow laws were state and local laws that enforced racial segregation in the South after Reconstruction ended. They separated people by race in schools, transportation, and public places for decades. The civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s finally forced the nation to dismantle them.

timelineEvents.title: Freedmen's Bureau Established
timelineEvents.description: Congress creates a federal agency to help formerly enslaved people with food, schools, and legal support

timelineEvents.title: Lincoln Assassinated
timelineEvents.description: Days after the war's end, John Wilkes Booth kills President Lincoln, leaving Reconstruction to Andrew Johnson

timelineEvents.title: 13th Amendment Ratified
timelineEvents.description: Slavery is abolished throughout the United States by constitutional amendment

timelineEvents.title: 14th Amendment Ratified
timelineEvents.description: Birthright citizenship and equal protection under the law are written into the Constitution

timelineEvents.title: 15th Amendment Ratified
timelineEvents.description: The Constitution bars states from denying the vote based on race, color, or previous enslavement

timelineEvents.title: Compromise of 1877 Ends Reconstruction
timelineEvents.description: The disputed 1876 election is settled: Hayes becomes president and federal troops leave the South
